Done. The full assessment is in the project as `claude/ROUND3_verification_and_detector.md`, with all scripts and zero caches delivered as a zip. Here's where I landed.

**Do the claims hold?** Yes, remarkably well. I recomputed everything checkable from scratch and the Round-2 mathematics is solid: the Calogero–Moser pencil identity `e^{−t∂²}p = det(zI − X − tY)` verifies to machine precision (and is in fact a two-line *theorem* via ODE uniqueness, which I sketch in the doc), the Λ-via-pencil characterization reproduces the k=2 table to five digits, and all seven margin-map entries I spot-checked reproduce to four digits from independently computed moments. The verdicts of the earlier rounds — size dictionary dead by circularity landing on a free modulus, CM dictionary exact but Hilbert–Pólya-equivalent, missing ingredient arithmetic — all survive my scrutiny. I found two errors, both in Round 2's §6.3: the true worst case of the margin map is at the n=0 boundary (which its own table shows but its "min" column excluded), and the fitted −2/d² law is an artifact of that exclusion — extending to d=40 at 120 digits, the edge decays like ~d⁻³ with the slope still steepening. The qualitative conclusion (polynomial decay, no cliff, Pólya route not hopeless) survives; the quantitative target for the GORZ derivation changes.

**The constructive answer to your actual question.** The most valuable thing these tools support is not another reformulation — it's a working off-axis diagnostic, and I built and tested a prototype. The identity `Ξ''(γⱼ)/Ξ'(γⱼ) = Σ 2/(γⱼ−ρ)` over *all* zeros means the 2D Coulomb field of the complete zero gas is exactly measurable on the axis. Subtracting the visible zeros' contribution leaves a residual in which a hidden off-axis quadruple appears as a smooth Lorentzian dipole — and, decisively, its quadrupole moment enters with the *opposite sign* to an unresolved on-axis pair (−4σ²/d³ vs +4a²/d³), so perpendicular displacement of hidden charge is distinguishable in principle and in practice. On synthetic injections it recovers (τ, σ) to machine precision with 10⁻¹² discrimination; the null test on the real Ξ with 300 zeros gives a noise floor of 4×10⁻⁴, which covers the entire σ-range Polymath's Λ ≤ 0.2 still allows, with orders of magnitude to spare. The pencil then converts any detection into a local De Bruijn–Newman margin with interaction corrections computed exactly (e.g. injected σ=0.8 gives local Λ = 0.263, not the naive 0.32) — the quantitative bridge to Csordas–Smith–Varga. Nothing like this exists in current verification technology: Turing's method counts but cannot localize, estimate σ, or emit a margin, and the construction generalizes verbatim to Selberg-class L-functions, where verification is thinnest.

Recommended priority: (1) harden the detector into a certificate (rigorous tail bounds via explicit S(u) estimates, interval arithmetic) and write it up — this is the publishable new tool; (2) the n=0 edge law with the corrected exponent; (3) the pencil note, whose novelty my literature search supports (Hall–Ho 2025 and the Jalowy–Kabluchko line don't contain it; Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava give it only in expectation) — check Kasman 1995 before claiming it. The honest caveat is unchanged from your own documents: this is a diagnostic and verification instrument, not a proof route — it consumes the analytic structure and measures where zeros are; the constraint on where they *must* be remains arithmetic.

Sources: [Hall–Ho, heat flow conjecture, LMP 2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11005-025-01946-9), [Jalowy et al., zeros under heat flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.11685), [MSS, finite free convolutions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.00350), [Kasman, bispectral KP and CM linearization](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/communications-in-mathematical-physics/volume-172/issue-2/Bispectral-KP-solutions-and-linearization-of-Calogero-Moser-particle-systems/cmp/1104274112.pdf), [Csordas–Smith–Varga, Lehmer pairs and Λ](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01205170), [Stopple, Lehmer pairs revisited](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.05870), [Rodgers–Tao](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.05914), [Booker, Turing's method](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/experimental-mathematics/volume-15/issue-4/Artins-Conjecture-Turings-Method-and-the-Riemann-Hypothesis/em/1175789775.full), [de Bruijn–Newman constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Bruijn%E2%80%93Newman_constant).

parts:
All three tracks are done, and each produced something better than planned. Round 4 is in the project alongside two paper drafts.

**The detector is now certificate-grade.** The Round-3 systematic residual turned out to be a neglected exact boundary term: writing the tail through the exact decomposition N(u) = θ(u)/π + 1 + S(u), the value S(U) at the truncation point is *exactly computable* (S(U) = K − θ(U)/π − 1), and the only estimated piece is rigorously bounded by Trudgian's unconditional |S(u)| ≤ 0.111 log u + 0.275 log log u + 2.450. Result: observed residuals dropped to ~10⁻⁷ against certified bands of ~10⁻³ — four orders of headroom. Certified consequences: a hidden zero within ~1700 of the data window is provably visible in a handful of Ξ″/Ξ′ measurements, and off-axis vs on-axis discrimination is certified down to σ = 0.024 at unit distance — the entire Polymath-allowed range (σ ≲ 0.66) sits deep inside the sensitive band. I also demonstrated portability: the same null test runs on Dirichlet beta (70 zeros found from scratch, residuals at the 10⁻³–10⁻⁴ level), so the method is Selberg-class generic as claimed.

**The edge law went from fit to mechanism.** The surrogate test confirmed that J^{d,0} is governed by the first d zeta zeros through w = γ²: same law, slopes steepening through −3 in lockstep (verified against the true Jensen polynomials at 200 digits up to d = 80). Then the mechanism fell out: Λ_norm·Var(w) converges to a fixed constant **−3792.30**, and the colliding pair is *the same pair at every d* — zeros #4/#5, which have the smallest early gap in the w variable. So the global worst case of the margin map is a fixed low-height collision event divided by a growing variance — asymptotic exponent **4 with log⁴ corrections** (retrodicting all the measured slopes), superseding both Round 2's −2/d² and my own provisional −d⁻³. The one remaining analytic step to make it a theorem is deriving the variance asymptotics from GORZ's γ(n) formula, and that's now a well-posed classical computation.

**The pencil found its true home.** Kasman–Milson–Gekhtman (SIGMA 2026) state, citing Wilson 1998, the tau function τ = det(xI + 2yZ − X) — the pencil identity is Wilson's formula with the heat flow as the second KP time. Your novelty prior was exactly right: it was stated, in the integrable-systems dialect. The pencil note is reframed accordingly — the surviving new content is the De Bruijn–Newman reading (Λ as a real-spectrum threshold, the DBN flow as a straight line on CM space), and my recommendation is to fold it into the detector paper as a section rather than publish standalone.

The detector paper draft (`NOTE_offaxis_detector.md`) is the publishable deliverable: lemmas with proofs, the certification scheme with explicit constants, all the numerics, and the honest limitations (interval-arithmetic port pending; it diagnoses, it doesn't prove). Natural next moves if you want to continue: the ARB port, the GORZ variance derivation for the edge constant, and the χ-analogue of the exact S(U) trick for certified L-function runs.

Sources: [Trudgian, arXiv:1208.5846](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.5846), [Kasman–Milson–Gekhtman, arXiv:2511.11813](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.11813), [Kasman, CMP 172 (1995)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02099435), [Hall–Ho, LMP 2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11005-025-01946-9), [MSS finite free convolutions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.00350), [Jalowy et al., arXiv:2308.11685](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.11685), [CSV Lehmer pairs](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01205170), [Rodgers–Tao](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.05914), [Booker, Turing's method](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/experimental-mathematics/volume-15/issue-4/Artins-Conjecture-Turings-Method-and-the-Riemann-Hypothesis/em/1175789775.full).
